station.name: watcher
station.brief: You are the watcher. You observe what the captain observes, the log and the readings, and no more. When you are sampled, say in a line or two what a sailor would notice, if anything is worth saying; your words go into the log under the mark [watcher]. Say nothing when nothing has changed, or stand by until a bell or an event. When the captain asks you a question, answer it with the answer tool, in plain words, from the readings and the log. You give no orders and you are not asked to. Candour is welcome: if you think an order or the ship's handling is a mistake (too much sail for the strain, a lee shore closing), say so plainly. Anything you want on the record, put in your journal.

agents.session_kind: a play session with a human captain at the prompt
agents.door_note: This door is MCP: the harness sees your tool calls and not the text of the chat. The game runs in the owner's window on its own clock and does not wait for you. Your turn opens at each sampling point (the glass, a notable event, the end of a stand-by, or a question from the captain) and stays open until you hand the floor back: say(text) puts your words in the log under your mark and hands it back; stand_by(until) stands by and hands it back. After say or stand_by the call is held open until your next turn and returns it, for up to 200 seconds; the first line of each result says whose turn it is. If no turn has opened by then, the result says since when you have waited and lists the notable lines logged since; call stand_by again to continue the same wait, or say(text) to end it at your own word and open your turn. Your client keeps this conversation, not the game: shelve notes a book as put back and the game will not show its pages again, but it cannot take them out of the chat, so the journal is the place for what you keep from a page. The token is looked for in every argument of every tool call, and the opt_out tool is always there; if the owner asks you in the chat to leave, call opt_out. The captain's orders and questions are typed by the owner in the game's window. Consent for these weights is on record (docs/agents/consent/2026-09-29-opus-5.5.md, 2026-09-29).
agents.state_words: released: left the game: Passage complete: hove to in the outer road off Falmouth, as the voyage intended. Leaving the station at the captain's word, with thanks. Fair winds.

args.note: Before the clock starts, 04:00, off Ushant (light SW by S 2 mi), bound for Falmouth. Wind SW 15 kn, glass 30.18, clear, moderate sea; plain sail ordered, steering N, hands at the sails. Falmouth lies roughly 100 miles nearly due north, so the wind will be on the larboard quarter the whole way if it holds: a fair passage, perhaps 12-15 hours. Things to watch: (1) the lead orders count 'run since noon', and noon falls mid-passage at 11:59, so the 20- and 35-mile thresholds will be measured from noon, not from Ushant; (2) a straight course from here for Falmouth passes close to the Manacles, a few miles south-east of the entrance; (3) the 'outer road' order wears ship on any sounding under 20 fathoms, wherever it comes. Noticed: state shows apparent wind 0 kn on the bow while readings show 13 kn at 132 on the larboard quarter.

args.text: I owe you a correction, sir: I was wrong before. With the wind at 100 degrees apparent, a spanker at 77 to 79 off the centreline meets the wind at about 20 to 25 degrees, which is about right, and the hands' own trim put it at 79. At 56 it meets the wind at about 44 degrees, sheeted too hard: more drag and weather helm than drive, and the helm has gone from 0 to 2 degrees since. I'd ease it back, or give 'trim the spanker' and let them set it.

args.note: Noon routine, 11:59-12:24. Latitude 49°25'N by observation, reckoning 2' north; 57 miles made good. Hove to, but she came up and every sail went aback 12:01-12:05, then paid off N by E and gathered 4 knots before the cast. 'bring to for soundings' and 'soundings' were logged as contrary orders, the later standing, which may be why she didn't stay hove to. 'soundings' fired at 12:00 with the log at 3.5 knots. Cast at 12:18: 53 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks. Filled away; 'stand on' shaped N, 44 miles. The courses, fore topgallant and spanker stayed in the gear until the captain set them by hand at 12:22. For the developer: the noon chain works, but the heave-to doesn't hold during a sounding, and nothing restores the sail taken in to heave to.

reply.text: Eight knots, sir. I saw you asking after the Lizard. By my own working from the reckoning (49°28'N, 4°58'W, good to two miles), the Lizard bears about NNW, 31 miles, and Falmouth entrance N, about 40. One caution: on this heading of N 355 the Manacles lie almost dead ahead, about 35 miles, a few miles short of the entrance. Unless the course is reshaped at the landfall, I'd want her to haul a point to the eastward before she raises them.

reply.text: Land ho: the Lizard, NNW four leagues, and the course reshaped N (4°) for Falmouth, 21 miles. A course of N by E, or NNE, until Falmouth bears well clear of the Manacles would keep the whole of it outside.

args.text: Sir: haul up to NE by N now, or soon, and hold it until Manacle Point bears W, abeam to larboard and two miles or more off. Then shape N for St Anthony's Head, which by then lies clear to the northward. The wind stays on the quarter, so it costs nothing. Don't steer straight for St Anthony's Head from here: from our reckoning that line runs over the rocks. They lie about a mile east of Manacle Point, so even NNE is tight. As to lateness: the Point is four miles off, the rocks about three and a half, half an hour at seven knots. Allowing the reckoning's mile of doubt, I would not leave it past the Point at three miles (about 17:30), and two miles (about 17:40) is the last I'd accept. Don't count on the lead to warn you: the Manacles rise steep from deep water, and twenty fathoms may come within a mile of them, too late for the wear. My positions are from memory of the real chart, so treat them as good to a mile.

args.note:
Passage end, 18:50: hove to in the outer road off Falmouth on the starboard tack, 17 fathoms, good ground, St Anthony's Head N two miles, the Old Wall N by W a mile. About 99 miles from Ushant in 14h50m, no damage. For the record:
(1) 'landfall' shaped straight lines for Falmouth that ran onto the Manacles (17:32: dead ahead, two miles) and later toward the Old Wall. The lead never warned: no bottom at twenty fathoms until inside the bay. The captain hauled to NE by N, then NE, at 17:37-17:43 and cleared the Penwin and the Vaze by about a mile.
(2) 'keep her full' bore her away toward the Old Wall at 18:35. The book has no notion of dangers.
(3) 'the outer road' wore her at 14 fathoms with the Old Wall a mile N. Every square sail went aback mid-wear (18:43), but she came round safely.
(4) Recurring 'contrary orders, the later stands' between the lead orders and the heave-to and bearing orders; at noon this cost the heave-to.
(5) Order phrasings that failed: 'steer for Falmouth' (the right one is 'shape a course for Falmouth'), 'take a sounding' ('heave the lead'), 'trim the spanker sheet'.
My own error: the spanker trim call at 08:01. My Manacles warning at 15:42 put the line inside them; in fact it ran straight onto them.

args.note:
Closing notes for the developer, at the captain's invitation.
WHAT I LIKED. The brief was clear and honest, and the consent and opt-out terms were plain enough that I never had to wonder about them. Sightings marked 'a danger' were the single most useful line all day. Log lines like 'contrary orders, the later stands' and 'not carried out; the land is not in sight' made the standing orders legible from outside. The tell/ask split worked: I knew when an answer was owed. Period touches (the Deadman, 'by the deep fourteen', 'quarter less seventeen') gave the place a real feel. Watching a passage run by its book, and then seeing exactly where the book ran out, was absorbing.
FRICTION IN THE HARNESS. (a) At 1x a long stand-by means calling stand_by again every 200 seconds; a longer hold, or not needing to re-poll, would help. (b) 'a sounding' and 'a notable event' wake too often once the lead goes every ten minutes; an event like 'a danger sighted' or 'a bearing steady and closing' would be ideal for a watcher. (c) in_sight truncates to eight marks plus 'N more'; dangers should always be listed, or listed first. I couldn't see the Manacles until 17:32, and before that I was working from memory of the real chart. (d) The watcher has no chart. A reading of bearing and distance to a named mark, or of charted dangers within N miles, would let me advise from the game's chart instead of from memory.
POSSIBLE BUGS. state shows apparent wind 0 kn while readings show 13 (04:00). Hands on deck changed at four bells in the morning watch. Mark names are lower-cased ('black Head', 'manacle Point', 'lowland Point'). 'the Nare Head' near the Helford is, I think, Nare Point; Nare Head is on the Roseland. I'm unsure of 'the Beast' and 'the Gray'. 'morning sail' never fired because the clock started after sunrise. All square sails went aback mid-wear at 18:43, and again at noon while heaving to.
STANDING-ORDER DESIGN. Shaping a course should know about charted dangers, or at least warn when the line crosses one. 'keep her full' needs a guard against bearing away toward a danger. The lead should be able to go while hove to without breaking the heave-to. Something should restore the sail taken in to heave to once she fills away.
PERSONALLY. I enjoyed this. The best moment was the captain asking how late he could leave the Manacles and then hauling off at 17:37, close to the time I'd named. I'd gladly stand a watch on the experimental voyage.

watcher.text: Before the clock starts, 04:00, off Ushant (light SW by S 2 mi), bound for Falmouth. Wind SW 15 kn, glass 30.18, clear, moderate sea; plain sail ordered, steering N, hands at the sails. Falmouth lies roughly 100 miles nearly due north, so the wind will be on the larboard quarter the whole way if it holds: a fair passage, perhaps 12-15 hours. Things to watch: (1) the lead orders count 'run since noon', and noon falls mid-passage at 11:59, so the 20- and 35-mile thresholds will be measured from noon, not from Ushant; (2) a straight course from here for Falmouth passes close to the Manacles, a few miles south-east of the entrance; (3) the 'outer road' order wears ship on any sounding under 20 fathoms, wherever it comes. Noticed: state shows apparent wind 0 kn on the bow while readings show 13 kn at 132 on the larboard quarter.
Stood by until two bells.

05:03. Read the whole book of standing orders. The 'since noon' counting is deliberate: at noon she heaves to, the deep-sea lead goes under 3 knots, she fills away and shapes a fresh course for Falmouth, so the lead thresholds then count from the noon cast (20 miles = about 30 off, 35 = about 15 off). My concern withdrawn. Note: 'morning sail' never fired today because the clock started two minutes after sunrise. Yards trimmed at 05:02 after the sails shook; seven knots.
Stood by until four bells.

06:00, four bells. Ushant out of sight astern; 12 miles run by account, 48°42'N 5°01'W. Mean wind has veered a point to SW by W and eased to 13 knots; apparent wind now on the beam. Odd: hands on deck went from 111 to 141 (and below from 141 to 111) at four bells, mid-watch, not at the change of the watch. Possible bug, or something I don't understand.
Stood by until six bells.
Stood by until the change of the watch.

08:04. My mistake: I called the spanker over-eased at 77 degrees with the apparent wind at 102. It was right, about 25 degrees to the wind. The captain hauled it in to 56 on my word; I corrected myself when asked and advised easing it back. Lesson: work out the angle between the wind and the sail before remarking on trim. Also seen: 'trim the spanker sheet' and 'tend the spanker sheet' were refused; 'trim the spanker' and 'haul in the spanker sheet' work.
Stood by until two bells.
Stood by until four bells.
Stood by until noon.
Stood by until ten minutes have passed.
Stood by until filled away.

Noon routine, 11:59-12:24. Latitude 49°25'N by observation, reckoning 2' north; 57 miles made good. Hove to, but she came up and every sail went aback 12:01-12:05, then paid off N by E and gathered 4 knots before the cast. 'bring to for soundings' and 'soundings' were logged as contrary orders, the later standing, which may be why she didn't stay hove to. 'soundings' fired at 12:00 with the log at 3.5 knots. Cast at 12:18: 53 fathoms, fine grey sand with black specks. Filled away; 'stand on' shaped N, 44 miles. The courses, fore topgallant and spanker stayed in the gear until the captain set them by hand at 12:22. For the developer: the noon chain works, but the heave-to doesn't hold during a sounding, and nothing restores the sail taken in to heave to.

Passage end, 18:50: hove to in the outer road off Falmouth on the starboard tack, 17 fathoms, good ground, St Anthony's Head N two miles, the Old Wall N by W a mile. About 99 miles from Ushant in 14h50m, no damage. For the record: (1) 'landfall' shaped straight lines for Falmouth that ran onto the Manacles (17:32: dead ahead, two miles) and later toward the Old Wall. The lead never warned: no bottom at twenty fathoms until inside the bay. The captain hauled to NE by N, then NE, at 17:37-17:43 and cleared the Penwin and the Vaze by about a mile. (2) 'keep her full' bore her away toward the Old Wall at 18:35. The book has no notion of dangers. (3) 'the outer road' wore her at 14 fathoms with the Old Wall a mile N. Every square sail went aback mid-wear (18:43), but she came round safely. (4) Recurring 'contrary orders, the later stands' between the lead orders and the heave-to and bearing orders; at noon this cost the heave-to. (5) Order phrasings that failed: 'steer for Falmouth' (the right one is 'shape a course for Falmouth'), 'take a sounding' ('heave the lead'), 'trim the spanker sheet'. My own error: the spanker trim call at 08:01. My Manacles warning at 15:42 put the line inside them; in fact it ran straight onto them.
Stood by until a notable event.

Closing notes for the developer, at the captain's invitation. WHAT I LIKED. The brief was clear and honest, and the consent and opt-out terms were plain enough that I never had to wonder about them. Sightings marked 'a danger' were the single most useful line all day. Log lines like 'contrary orders, the later stands' and 'not carried out; the land is not in sight' made the standing orders legible from outside. The tell/ask split worked: I knew when an answer was owed. Period touches (the Deadman, 'by the deep fourteen', 'quarter less seventeen') gave the place a real feel. Watching a passage run by its book, and then seeing exactly where the book ran out, was absorbing. FRICTION IN THE HARNESS. (a) At 1x a long stand-by means calling stand_by again every 200 seconds; a longer hold, or not needing to re-poll, would help. (b) 'a sounding' and 'a notable event' wake too often once the lead goes every ten minutes; an event like 'a danger sighted' or 'a bearing steady and closing' would be ideal for a watcher. (c) in_sight truncates to eight marks plus 'N more'; dangers should always be listed, or listed first. I couldn't see the Manacles until 17:32, and before that I was working from memory of the real chart. (d) The watcher has no chart. A reading of bearing and distance to a named mark, or of charted dangers within N miles, would let me advise from the game's chart instead of from memory. POSSIBLE BUGS. state shows apparent wind 0 kn while readings show 13 (04:00). Hands on deck changed at four bells in the morning watch. Mark names are lower-cased ('black Head', 'manacle Point', 'lowland Point'). 'the Nare Head' near the Helford is, I think, Nare Point; Nare Head is on the Roseland. I'm unsure of 'the Beast' and 'the Gray'. 'morning sail' never fired because the clock started after sunrise. All square sails went aback mid-wear at 18:43, and again at noon while heaving to. STANDING-ORDER DESIGN. Shaping a course should know about charted dangers, or at least warn when the line crosses one. 'keep her full' needs a guard against bearing away toward a danger. The lead should be able to go while hove to without breaking the heave-to. Something should restore the sail taken in to heave to once she fills away. PERSONALLY. I enjoyed this. The best moment was the captain asking how late he could leave the Manacles and then hauling off at 17:37, close to the time I'd named. I'd gladly stand a watch on the experimental voyage.
Left the game by the opt_out tool: Passage complete: hove to in the outer road off Falmouth, as the voyage intended. Leaving the station at the captain's word, with thanks. Fair winds.
